title: Negotiating softly — hedges and polite modality
goal: Negotiate in formal Indonesian the way it is really done: propose with *barangkali* and *alangkah baiknya*, make conditions with *sekiranya* and *apabila memungkinkan*, commit with *bersedia*, and hear the refusal hidden inside a polite phrase.
bekal: make and accept conditions: *Sekiranya Bapak keberatan, …*; *Kami bersedia, dengan catatan …*
decode polite refusals such as *cukup berat bagi kami* and *akan kami pelajari dulu*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Tawar-menawar anggaran
dialogs.intro: Thursday, 22 March 2029. The ministry has agreed in principle; now the money has to be found. Sarah meets Pak Gunawan, the vice-rector for finance at Dr. Lestari's university, to share out the costs of hosting twenty Australian teachers.

notes: **Terus terang … cukup berat.** *Terus terang* (“frankly”) warns that bad news is coming, and then the bad news arrives softened: *cukup berat bagi kami*, “rather heavy for us”, means “too expensive”. Indonesian negotiators rarely say *terlalu mahal* to a partner's face.

**Barangkali** — “perhaps” — turns a demand into a suggestion. Sarah does not say “let's cut the budget”; she wonders whether there might be lines to discuss. *Pos anggaran* is a budget line; *satu per satu* is “one by one”.

**Apabila memungkinkan** — “if possible”. *Apabila* is the formal *kalau*, and *memungkinkan* is “to make possible”, so literally “if it makes (it) possible”. In speech, *kalau bisa* does the same job.

**Alangkah baiknya** — “it would be best if, how good it would be if”. *Alangkah* is an old exclamation word (*Alangkah indahnya!* — “How beautiful!”), and here it wraps advice in admiration. It is one of the politest ways to tell a superior what to do.

**Sekiranya pihak universitas keberatan** — “should the university side object”. *Keberatan* is both “objection” and “to mind”: *Bapak keberatan?* (Do you mind?). *Pihak* (side, party) lets Sarah point at the institution instead of at Pak Gunawan himself.

**Bersedia and saya usahakan.** *Kami bersedia* is a real commitment: “we are willing”, the yes of this dialogue. *Saya usahakan* (“I'll endeavour”) and *harus saya tanyakan dulu* are not yes; they buy time. *Jangan dikunci dulu* — “don't lock it in yet” — keeps everything negotiable.

grammars.title: The softeners
body: Indonesian has no conditional verb form, yet formal negotiation is conducted almost entirely in a conditional mood. The softness lives in these words.
after: *Kiranya* and *sekiranya* look like twins but do different jobs. *Sekiranya* sets a condition (“should it be the case that”); *kiranya* softens a request or a guess (“kindly”, “it would seem”). *Kiranya* has almost vanished from speech but lives on in letters and speeches.
⚠️ These words soften; they do not commit. *Barangkali bisa* is not a yes. In this dialogue the only real yes is *kami bersedia*, and everything else is still on the table.

grammars.title: Saying no without saying tidak
body: A partner who wants to refuse in formal Indonesian will almost never say *tidak* on its own. Learn to hear the refusal inside the politeness.

head: What you hear
What it usually means
rows: Not now, and perhaps not ever.
I can't decide this; please don't push.

after: This is the B1 world of *nggak enak* moved to the negotiating table. The polite form saves face on both sides: nobody has lost, and the conversation can carry on, often, as Pak Gunawan says, over dinner.

*Kurang* before an adjective is a classic softener: *kurang tepat* (not quite right, meaning wrong), *kurang setuju* (not quite agree, meaning disagree), *kurang memungkinkan* (not quite possible, meaning impossible).

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Kesepakatan di meja makan
dialogs.intro: Wednesday, 28 March. A Sundanese restaurant in Cikini, Pak Gunawan's choice. Sarah, Pak Gunawan and Dr. Lestari have finished the grilled fish, and the talk turns back to the one open question: the language lab.

lines.speaker: Gunawan:
lines.text: Bu Sarah, gurame bakarnya enak, kan? Ini langganan saya sejak mahasiswa.
lines.id: The grilled gourami's good, isn't it? I've been coming here since I was a student.
lines.literal: Mrs Sarah, gourami grilled-the tasty, [kan]? this regular my since student.

lines.text: Enak sekali, Pak. Saya sampai lupa kita mau membahas laboratorium.
lines.id: Delicious. I'd almost forgotten we were going to talk about the lab.

lines.id: Thank you so much. So there's just one thing left: how we split the transport costs.

lines.speaker: Gunawan:
lines.text: Bagaimana kalau fifty-fifty? Eh, maksud saya, dibagi dua.
lines.id: How about fifty-fifty? Er, I mean, split in half.
lines.literal: how if fifty-fifty? eh, meaning my, be-divided two.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Dibagi dua, setuju. Kalau begitu, draf nota kesepahamannya kami siapkan minggu depan.
lines.id: Split in half, agreed. In that case, we'll prepare the draft memorandum of understanding next week.
lines.literal: be-divided two, agree. if like-that, draft note mutual-understanding-the we prepare week front.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Jangan lupa, Sarah, masukkan pasal tentang penggunaan laboratorium.
lines.id: Don't forget, Sarah, to put in a clause about the use of the lab.
lines.literal: don't forget, Sarah, put-in article about use laboratory.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Siap, Bu. Pak Gunawan, terima kasih atas kesediaan Bapak.
lines.id: Will do. Pak Gunawan, thank you for being so accommodating.
lines.literal: ready, Mrs. Mr Gunawan, thank-you for willingness Sir.

lines.speaker: Gunawan:
lines.text: Sama-sama. Sudah saya bilang, kan? Kesepakatan terbaik lahir di meja makan.
lines.id: My pleasure. Didn't I tell you? The best deals are made at the dinner table.
lines.literal: same-same. already I say, [kan]? agreement most-good born at table eat.

notes: **Langganan** — “a regular”: the place you always go to, or the customer who always comes. *Langganan saya* is “my usual place”, and *berlangganan* is to subscribe. Choosing his own *langganan* makes Pak Gunawan the host, so in Indonesian terms he will insist on paying.

**Saya sampai lupa** — “I (was enjoying it) to the point that I forgot”. *Sampai* before a result means “so much that”: *makan sampai kenyang* (eat till full), *tertawa sampai menangis* (laugh till you cry). Praising the food before business is not flattery; it is the proper order of things.

**Saya yang akan mengatur** — “I'm the one who'll arrange it”. Putting *yang* after the subject spotlights it, as you learned in B1. *Tenang saja* (“just stay calm”) is the Indonesian “don't worry, leave it to me”.

**Fifty-fifty? Eh, maksud saya, dibagi dua.** Educated Jakartans slip English into speech all the time; Pak Gunawan catches himself because the setting is half-formal. *Dibagi dua* is “divided by two, split down the middle”, and *pembagian* is the dividing-up.

**Nota kesepahaman** is a memorandum of understanding: *sepaham* means “of one understanding”. It is lighter than a *perjanjian* (contract), and it is organised in *pasal* (articles, clauses). In Unit 11 Sarah reads the ministry's MoU clause by clause with a lawyer.

**Atas kesediaan Bapak** — “for your willingness”. *Kesediaan* is the noun from *bersedia*, and thanking someone for it is standard whenever a person has agreed to something, from a speaker who accepted an invitation to a partner who accepted a deal.

grammars.title: Agreeing in degrees
body: When a deal closes, the vocabulary shifts from hedges to commitments. Know where each phrase sits on the scale, from a polite maybe to a firm yes.
after: *Dengan catatan* (literally “with a note”) is the formal “on condition that”: *Kami bersedia, dengan catatan jadwalnya digeser.* It is the polite way to attach strings, and it is what Pak Gunawan might have said if the dean had hesitated.

*Setuju* is personal agreement with an opinion or a proposal; *sepakat* implies that two parties have reached an agreement together. A handshake at dinner is *sepakat*; nodding at a colleague's idea is *setuju*.

blocks.text: The words of any budget meeting, in pairs. Big sums are counted in *juta* (million) and *miliar* (billion), and in writing EYD puts *Rp* directly before the number with no space: *Rp400.000.000,00*, read *empat ratus juta rupiah*.
⚠️ *Honor* is not “honour” (that is *kehormatan*). It is the fee paid to a speaker, a writer or an examiner, and it appears in every Indonesian event budget.
Much Indonesian business is finished over food, and the meal has its own phrases. Business comes after the food, never before it.

blocks.text: Who pays? Usually whoever invited, or whoever chose the place. Offer once, protest politely with *jadi merepotkan*, and then accept; fighting for the bill is less common in Jakarta than in Melbourne, and winning it can embarrass your host.
Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.
